chapter: Southwestern bands and New Orleans youth
title: Playing professional jobs as a boy, lake boats and the nine o'clock whistle
summary: His parents let him play jobs at about fourteen, and boat trips across the lake; his father blew a whistle to call him home.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well, as a kid, could you get out late at night or anything?
Well, my daddy would let me go with all the musicians and they would take me home.

Well, you were playing professional jobs quite young is what I'm getting to. About fourteen years old. And so you wouldn't get arrested then? Oh, no. No laws against working with the kid? No, no laws against working with the kid.
Your father then must have known the people you went out with. Oh, yes, you know.
So did my mother. And sometimes she came over and waited for me to take me home. For instance, when the boat docked over on this side of the lake where she or my daddy would be waiting for me.
What time would the boat get back?

Those hours were very vague in my mind. If I can remember well, they'd leave early in the morning. They would get over to Mandeville or Covington and they would spend three or four hours over there. The people would get off the boat and go around town and then picnics underneath the trees. Then they would leave and it seems as though the boat would get back here between six and seven o'clock just about dusk.
So you didn't have to worry about the nine o'clock bell?
Was there really a nine o'clock bell?
Yes, it was. When I was courting my wife, I was ready to get engaged to my wife and at nine o'clock, if I wasn't home, my daddy was on the corner blowing that whistle for me to get home.
